passage: Every school morning that week, Zubin curled up on the sofa of their Pune flat, clutching his middle. "My tummy hurts, Mumma." On Sunday it never hurt. Vandana's first thought was that he was pretending, and she almost said so. Instead she sat beside him and rubbed his back. "Tummies sometimes hurt when we're worried. Is anything at school worrying you?" Zubin was quiet, then whispered, "The new bus. I don't know anyone." Vandana held him close. "Let's find one friend's name together." If the aches kept coming, she decided, they would see the doctor too.

qa.q: What did Zubin say was worrying him?
qa.a: The new bus; Zubin said he did not know anyone.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling on school mornings?
qa.a: Zubin felt worried and scared about the new bus, and the worry showed up as a real tummy ache.

qa.q: Which choice helped Vandana learn what was wrong?
qa.a: Vandana sat beside Zubin and gently asked about worries instead of arguing that he was pretending, so he could tell her.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had told Zubin he was pretending?
qa.a: Zubin would likely have felt unbelieved and kept quiet about the bus, and the tummy aches would have gone on.

grounding: A young child's worry about school comes out as real tummy aches, and gentle talk about the fear works better than arguing.

passage:
"Papa, my tummy's sore again."
"Tarun, it's Monday. You were fine at the park yesterday. Shoes on."
"It hurts." Tarun sat on the floor and cried harder.
Vijay stopped, then knelt beside his son. "Okay. I believe you. Where does it hurt?"
"Here. It feels squeezy."
"Sometimes a squeezy tummy means we're worried. Is something at school scary?"
"Ma'am shouts when our table is noisy. I'm in the noisy one."
"That sounds scary." Vijay stroked his hair. "Shall I walk you in, and we tell Ma'am together that loud voices squeeze your tummy?"
Tarun nodded, sniffing, and found his shoes.

qa.q: What does Tarun say his tummy feels like?
qa.a: Tarun says it feels squeezy.

qa.q: Why did Tarun cry harder when told to put his shoes on?
qa.a: Tarun felt unbelieved and scared; the pain was real, and being brushed off made him more upset.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Vijay argued that Tarun had been fine yesterday, which made Tarun cry; kneeling, believing him and asking gently about school fears helped.

qa.q: How did Vijay's view of the tummy ache change during the talk?
qa.a: Vijay first saw it as a Monday excuse, but after kneeling and listening he saw it as real worry about the noisy table.

grounding: A young child's school worry is felt as a real tummy ache, and gentle talk about the fear helps more than arguing about whether it is true.

passage: Every Monday, Jeevan's tummy hurt. He lay on the sofa of their Chennai flat, holding his belly, while Urmila packed his bag. Last week she had snapped, 'You're fine, it's just school.' This Monday she sat beside him instead and rubbed his back. 'Where does it hurt, kanna?' He pointed. 'Does anything at school feel scary?' Jeevan was quiet. Then: 'The new teacher shouts. What if she shouts at me?' Urmila held him close. 'That sounds worrying. Your tummy is telling us you're worried.' She promised to meet the teacher that afternoon. Jeevan sat up and ate half his idli.

qa.q: What did Jeevan eat after talking to Urmila?
qa.a: Half his idli.

qa.q: What was Jeevan really worried about?
qa.a: He was scared that the new teacher, who shouts, would shout at him.

qa.q: What worked better than last week's approach?
qa.a: Sitting with him, asking gently about school and treating his tummy ache as real, instead of saying he was fine.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel about last week's snapping now?
qa.a: She may feel a little sorry, now that she understands the tummy ache was carrying a real fear.

grounding: Shows a young child whose worry about school shows up as a real tummy ache, and a parent whose gentle questions help more than arguing.

passage:
'Papa, my tummy hurts. I can't go.'
'Jomon, you said that yesterday. You're not sick.'
'It does hurt!' Jomon's lip wobbled.
Lokesh knelt down. 'Okay. I believe you. Show me where.'
Jomon pressed a hand on his middle.
'Tight or sharp?'
'Tight. Like a knot.'
'Sometimes a knot means we're worried. Is something at school worrying you?'
Jomon whispered, 'Sports day. I have to run in front of everyone.'
'That is a big thing.' Lokesh hugged him. 'Shall we practise running in the park this evening?'
Jomon nodded. The knot loosened a bit.

qa.q: What did Jomon say the tummy ache felt like?
qa.a: Tight. Like a knot.

qa.q: What was Jomon afraid of?
qa.a: He was nervous about running in front of everyone on sports day.

qa.q: What turned the morning around?
qa.a: Lokesh stopped arguing, said he believed Jomon and asked gentle questions until the worry came out.

qa.q: How was the start of the talk different for Lokesh and Jomon?
qa.a: Lokesh first heard an excuse he had heard yesterday, while Jomon felt a real pain and felt disbelieved.

grounding: Shows a young child's worry about school appearing as a real tummy ache, and how gentle talk works better than arguing about whether it is true.

passage:
Note for Pranav's parents
For two weeks Pranav has come to me at drop-off holding his tummy. It starts right as Mummy leaves the gate, and by snack time he is playing happily. Today I sat with him on the reading mat. 'Your tummy feels bad. I believe you. Sometimes tummies hurt when we're worried. Is something worrying you?' He whispered, 'What if Mummy forgets to come back?' Could we try a goodbye plan: a hug, a wave from the window, and your photo in his pocket? Please check with your doctor if the aches come at other times too.
Vidya, KG teacher

qa.q: When does Pranav's tummy ache start?
qa.a: Right as Mummy leaves the gate.

qa.q: What was Pranav worried about?
qa.a: He was scared that Mummy would forget to come back.

qa.q: What plan did Vidya suggest?
qa.a: A goodbye plan: a hug, a wave from the window and his parents' photo in his pocket.

qa.q: How might Pranav's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel relieved to understand the aches and a little sad that he has been so worried at drop-off.

grounding: Shows a young child's worry about separation appearing as a real tummy ache, and a teacher who believes the pain and talks gently about the fear.

passage: Every morning that week in their village near Nashik, Ira clutched her tummy when the school rickshaw honked. 'Aai, it hurts!' On Sunday it never hurt. Her grandmother muttered that she was pretending. Urmila, her mother, didn't argue about whether it was real. She sat Ira on her lap on the doorstep and asked, 'What happens at school that feels scary?' Ira whispered that the new teacher shouted and she was afraid to ask for the toilet. Urmila rubbed her back. 'That's a big worry for a small tummy.' That afternoon Urmila met the teacher, and they agreed on a simple hand signal for the toilet.

qa.q: What signal did Urmila and the teacher agree on?
qa.a: A simple hand signal for the toilet.

qa.q: What was Ira worried about at school?
qa.a: She was afraid of the new teacher's shouting and scared to ask for the toilet.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's approach help more than arguing?
qa.a: She treated the pain as real, gently asked about fears, and fixed the worry with the teacher that same afternoon.

qa.q: How did Ira's grandmother see the tummy aches?
qa.a: She thought Ira was pretending, since it never hurt on Sundays.

grounding: A young child's school-morning tummy aches carry a worry she has no words for, and gentle talk about fears helps.
